tagline: Two oceans and a thousand shades of green
overview:
Colombia sits at the top corner of South America, the only country on the continent with coasts on both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea. It borders Panama, Venezuela, Brazil, Peru and Ecuador and covers about 1.14 million km², nearly twice the size of Texas. Around 52 million people live there, most of them in the cool Andean highlands and along the Caribbean coast.

The capital, Bogotá, sprawls across a plateau 2,640 meters up in the mountains. Medellín, Cali and Cartagena, a walled colonial port on the Caribbean, are other major cities. Spanish is the national language, and Colombians are famous for their warmth, their music and their coffee.

Colombia is a republic with an elected president. It is the second most biodiverse country on Earth after Brazil, with more kinds of birds and orchids than any other nation. After decades of armed conflict between the government, guerrilla groups and drug cartels, a 2016 peace agreement brought new hope, and tourists now flock to its beaches, cities and jungles.
landAndNature:
The Andes split into three parallel ranges as they enter Colombia, creating deep valleys and high plateaus where most people live. East of the mountains lie the wide grasslands of the Llanos and then the Amazon rainforest, which covers about a third of the country. The Pacific coast is one of the rainiest places on Earth, and humpback whales come there each year to give birth.

Colombia has about 1,900 species of birds, more than any other country, from hummingbirds to the Andean condor, plus poison dart frogs, pink river dolphins, spectacled bears and jaguars. Wax palms, the tallest palm trees in the world at up to 60 meters, tower over the Cocora Valley. Caño Cristales, a river in the Serranía de la Macarena, blazes red, yellow and green for a few months each year because of an aquatic plant.
peopleAndCulture:
Colombians are a mix of Indigenous, Spanish and African heritage, and each region has its own flavor. Along the Caribbean coast, cumbia and vallenato accordion music set the rhythm; Cali calls itself the world capital of salsa dancing. The Barranquilla Carnival, one of the largest in the world, and Medellín's Festival of Flowers fill the streets with parades.

Arepas, grilled corn cakes, are eaten at every meal, along with ajiaco chicken soup in Bogotá and the enormous bandeja paisa platter of beans, rice, meat, plantain and avocado. Colombian coffee is prized around the world. Soccer is the national passion, and cycling is close behind, with Colombian riders winning major European races. The writer Gabriel García Márquez won the Nobel Prize in 1982 for novels full of magical realism, and singer Shakira is a global star.
history:
Ancient cultures such as the Tayrona, who built the stone terraces of the Lost City, and the Muisca, whose golden offerings in Lake Guatavita inspired the legend of El Dorado, thrived long before Europeans came. Spanish settlers founded Santa Marta in 1525 and Cartagena in 1533, which became a major port for gold and for enslaved Africans.

Independence fighters led by Simón Bolívar defeated the Spanish at the Battle of Boyacá in 1819, creating Gran Colombia, a union that included Venezuela and Ecuador until it broke apart in 1831. Panama separated in 1903. In the 1900s Colombia suffered civil violence, and from the 1960s a long war involving guerrilla groups, paramilitaries and drug cartels killed hundreds of thousands. A 2016 peace accord with the largest guerrilla group, the FARC, began a slow recovery.
funFacts: Colombia is named after Christopher Columbus, even though he never set foot on its land.
Most of the world's emeralds come from Colombian mines, and the finest are deep, glowing green.
Every Sunday, Bogotá closes more than 100 kilometers of streets to cars so people can bike and skate, a tradition since 1974.
Colombia grows and ships more cut flowers than any country except the Netherlands, mostly roses and carnations.
The national sport, tejo, involves throwing a metal disc at targets packed with small gunpowder charges that explode on impact.
Colombia is the only South American country with coasts on both the Pacific and the Caribbean.
